title: Section check: Truth, power and choices
intro: 10 questions about Lessons 13–17. Take your time. You can look back at the lessons and try again as often as you like.

questions.question: A picture has an extra finger. Why is that only a clue, not proof, that AI made it?

options.text: Only artists can spot an extra finger
options.feedback: Not quite. Anyone can spot it. But real photos can look strange too. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: Real photos can look odd too
options.feedback: Yes. Real photos can look strange, for example in poor light. And newer AI tools make fewer mistakes.

options.text: AI tools never make that kind of mistake
options.feedback: Not quite. AI pictures sometimes have an extra finger. But a real photo can look odd too. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.question: In a 2025 study, more than 50,000 people judged real photos and AI pictures. What did it find?

options.text: People made many mistakes, both ways
options.feedback: Yes. They called about one in four real photos AI-made. They also missed about one in four AI pictures.

options.text: People spotted almost every AI picture
options.feedback: Not quite. They missed about one in four AI pictures. Look back at Lesson 13.

options.text: Real photos were always easy to tell
options.feedback: Not quite. People called about one in four real photos AI-made. Look back at Lesson 13.

questions.question: “The bridge closes for a whole year” is a claim. What is a claim?

options.text: A fact that has already been checked
options.feedback: Not quite. A claim may not be checked yet. It may be true or false. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: A post that many people have shared
options.feedback: Not quite. Sharing does not make something a claim, or make it true. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: Something a person says is true
options.feedback: Yes. A claim is something a person says is true. It may be true or false, so you check it.

stimulus.title: A made-up post in Rockford
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. In the made-up town of Rockford, a page with no name posts: “The market closes forever on Monday. Share this before they delete it.” There is no link and no evidence. Three other pages copy the post word for word.

questions.question: Which source would best show if the post is true?

options.text: The town office that runs the market
options.feedback: Yes. The office runs the market, so it knows the plans. Check what it says before you share.

options.text: The three pages that copied the post
options.feedback: Not quite. Copies add no evidence. Four copies are still one source. Look back at Lesson 14.

options.text: How many times the post was shared
options.feedback: Not quite. A shocking post can be shared a lot and still be false. Look back at Lesson 14.

questions.question: Some people worry that a feed shows each of us only one side of things. What is this called?

options.text: A news alert
options.feedback: Not quite. A news alert tells you about one new story. It is not about seeing only one side. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: A filter bubble
options.feedback: Yes. In a filter bubble, you only see one side. A 2022 review found that real bubbles are less common than many think.

options.text: An algorithm
options.feedback: Not quite. An algorithm is a set of steps that picks posts. It is not the one-sided feed itself. Look back at Lesson 15.

questions.question: In Maplebrook, a post said the vote had moved to Friday. It got 900 shares. The election office's post got 60. What does this show?

options.text: Most people checked the post before sharing it
options.feedback: Not quite. The false post got far more shares than the true ones. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: The vote really did move to Friday
options.feedback: Not quite. The election office and the fact-checkers say the vote is still on Saturday. Look back at Lesson 15.

options.text: A rumour can spread further than the truth
options.feedback: Yes. The rumour had no name and no link, but it got far more shares than the true post.

questions.question: How does the European Union's AI Act sort the ways AI is used?

options.text: By how much harm they could do
options.feedback: Yes. The law sorts uses by risk. Some uses are banned, and some need strict checks.

options.text: By which company made the tool
options.feedback: Not quite. The law looks at risk: how much harm a use could do. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: By how new or old each tool is
options.feedback: Not quite. Age does not matter in this law. It sorts uses by risk. Look back at Lesson 16.

stimulus.title: A made-up town meeting
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. The council of the made-up town of Lakeford plans a chatbot to answer questions at night. A student group is getting ready for the town meeting. They write down questions to look into.

questions.question: Which of their questions asks for a recommendation, not a fact?

options.text: Since 2026, what must EU chatbots make clear?
options.feedback: Not quite. The EU law gives a factual answer: a chatbot must make clear that it is a machine. Look back at Lesson 16.

options.text: Should Lakeford's chatbot work at night?
options.feedback: Yes. This asks what Lakeford should do. Your view can be different from any law, if you give reasons.

options.text: Is the ASEAN guide a law or a guideline?
options.feedback: Not quite. This has a factual answer: the ASEAN guide is a guideline. Look back at Lesson 16.

questions.question: What would a project need to show impact?

options.text: A prize from a big group of judges
options.feedback: Not quite. A prize shows that judges liked an idea. It does not show that life got better. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: A first working version of it
options.feedback: Not quite. That is a prototype. Impact comes later, if there is evidence that it helps. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Evidence that it made life better
options.feedback: Yes. Impact is the real difference a project makes. SELENA+ does not have that evidence yet.

stimulus.title: A made-up design team
stimulus.body: This is a made-up example. At the made-up Elm Street Centre, many visitors get lost in the big building. Pita wants to build an AI helper to guide them. Noor says, “Clear signs on the walls might work better.”

questions.question: What does Lesson 17 say about Noor's idea?

options.text: A simpler plan can be a strong design
options.feedback: Yes. First decide if AI should be used at all. A sign, a rule or a person can be a better answer.

options.text: Every good design needs to use AI
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says a sign, a simple rule or a person can be better. Look back at Lesson 17.

options.text: Signs are only for very small buildings
options.feedback: Not quite. The lesson says a simpler plan, with reasons, is a strong design. Look back at Lesson 17.

results.high: Well done. You know how to check what you see, and how people make rules and plans for AI.
results.middle: Good work. You got many questions right. Look back at the lessons for the ones you missed, and try again if you like.
results.low: Thank you for trying. Look back at Lessons 13–17, then try again. You can take as long as you need.
